Ethical dilemmas: when principles conflict — a choice between two or more defensible actions, with an original example stated simply

The nurse's role: advocate for the patient, stated simply
The honest framing: ethics is the compass for hard days — the reality check that most daily decisions are clear-cut and the hard cases are the exception

claims.claim: Ethics is a branch of philosophy — a set of moral principles, virtues, or ideals that guide behavior and help distinguish right from wrong — and nursing ethics provide the moral base from which nurses work; ethics are embedded in everything nurses do. Working definition for this lesson: ethics in healthcare is the set of principles that guide right action in care.

The ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses ('the Code') is the definitive standard for ethical nursing practice in the United States; it guides nurses as they make patient care and practice decisions, and the ANA states that ethics are fundamental to the integrity of the nursing profession because life-and-death decisions are a part of nursing.

The most recent version of the Code of Ethics for Nurses was published in 2015 and reaffirmed in the fourth edition of the ANA Scope and Standards for Nursing Practice (2021); the ANA states that the Code evolves to address today's pressing healthcare demands — the honest note that the Code is a living document.

The four main ethical principles are autonomy (patients should have the right to make their own decisions), beneficence (nurses should do good for the benefit of others), nonmaleficence (nurses should do no harm either intentionally or unintentionally and protect those who cannot protect themselves), and justice (treat all people equally and judge them on the same criteria no matter who they are, what their illness is, or how much money they have).

An ethical dilemma occurs when there must be a choice between two or more actions that are equally good, equally bad, or of unknown benefit — often because ethical principles pull in different directions; nurses work through dilemmas using decision-making strategies, nursing values, standards, and the Code of Ethics.

A facility's ethics committee is a group that works together on a regular basis to address ethical issues within the organization; it usually includes providers, nurses, chaplains, legal representation, and sometimes community members, and nurses should use it when they have questions or concerns about whether a situation is fully ethical.
Many healthcare agencies have chaplains onsite who offer patients a spiritual resource.

Every day, nurses support each other to fulfill their ethical obligations to patients and the public (ANA), and ethical decision-making happens alone or as part of the healthcare team (OpenStax) — colleagues are part of how nurses work through ethics.

Advocacy — publicly lending one's voice and/or support to a cause, person, or policy — is a core component of professional nursing; nursing advocacy includes protecting patients from unintentional or intentional harm, teaching patients and families, ensuring the patient's wishes and needs are understood, and speaking out against injustice.
Most day-in and day-out decisions a nurse makes are very clear-cut in terms of their ethics; hard cases are the exception, and ethics is the framework that guides action through them.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Some nursing texts list more than four ethical principles: confidentiality, accountability, fidelity, and veracity appear alongside autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice.
positions: OpenStax 16.2 lists eight principles including confidentiality, accountability, fidelity, and veracity
This lesson's scope teaches the four main principles (autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice) and notes that some lists extend further
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Taught the four main principles as the core set (per the assignment scope); the lesson notes that some lists add more principles and that confidentiality has its own sibling topic.
